title: The Upgrade of Minescout Life and Its Web Presence — Part 2: The Rest of the Stack
summary: A look at v5, v6, and everything beyond Life — the portfolio, Minescout AI, the Beta mainframe, and what's coming next.
content:
What v5 Actually Added

Part 1 ended at v4 — year filtering, corrected dates, 32 posts confirmed. v5 was where things got interesting, because instead of fixing something broken, it added something new: a community layer. The reasoning was simple. It seemed like it would be fun for people reading to actually be able to react.

So it got comments. User accounts. Thumbs-up and thumbs-down ratings on every post. The implementation used the same Vite server plugin that already handled /api/save-post — it just grew three new endpoint groups. /api/register and /api/login for user accounts, with SHA-256 hashed passwords stored in a local data/users.json. /api/comments for per-post comments stored in data/comments.json. /api/ratings for votes stored in data/ratings.json. The entire user system lives in two flat files on disk. No database. Same pattern as the post API.

The login page grew from a single admin password field into a three-mode form: Sign In, Register, and Admin. The first two hit the new user endpoints. Admin still uses the session-based check from v1. Users stay logged in through sessionStorage — close the tab and you're signed out. No refresh tokens, no expiry logic, no complexity that wasn't necessary.

The admin panel also got a Comments tab in v5, where every comment across every post appears in one list and can be deleted. And the AI summary button that had been stubbed out since v2 finally did something — it hits the Cloudflare Worker, asks it to write a one-sentence card teaser from the post title and content, and puts the result directly in the summary field.

v6 — Fixing What v5 Broke

The pattern held. v5 added it, v6 fixed it. Comments.jsx became its own component — it had been inlined inside PostPage since v5 landed, which made it hard to reuse and harder to reason about. useUser.js became a proper hook. The favicon got updated to a PNG because the SVG was rendering inconsistently in some browsers. Beyond the structural cleanup, v6 was stabilization: a bug in the comment submission flow, vote state not persisting correctly across page navigation, edge cases in the login form. None of it was dramatic. It was the version where everything v5 had added actually worked reliably.

The AI That Runs the Sidebar

Both the AI Reflection module in the sidebar and the summary generator in the admin panel call the same endpoint: a Cloudflare Worker running on Llama 3 through Cloudflare's Workers AI — 100,000 free requests a day, which makes it free to run at this scale. The sidebar module sends the titles and categories of the eight most recent posts and asks for one or two sentences about momentum. The summary generator sends the post title, category, and the first 400 characters of content and asks for a card teaser under 20 words. Temperature is 0.3 on both. Neither is doing anything sophisticated. The point is that the sidebar would otherwise just be navigation and a heatmap, and something that actually responds to what's been posted lately makes it feel different from a static widget.

The Portfolio

Life is one piece of a larger web presence. The root — minescout.net — is the personal portfolio. It's a vanilla JS single-page app with no framework and no build step: one index.html, an app.js that handles routing and sidebar state, and a views.js that returns HTML strings for each route. It doesn't use Firebase for anything. The whole thing renders from that one views.js file — the same basic SPA pattern as Life, just without the React layer. It covers the work, a resume, a blog, an about page, and a /now page that gets updated whenever something changes (last updated August 1, 2026).

Minescout AI

The name is a little misleading. Minescout AI at minescout.net/ai is a web development service, not a product. The pitch is a clean slate rebuild — you send a link to your old site or one you like, and it gets thrown out and rebuilt from scratch as a fast, custom-coded single-page app. No plugins, no WordPress, nothing to manage. Turnaround is typically under a week depending on complexity. The "AI" part is a chatbot that can be trained on a client's specific business — their hours, services, pricing — and deployed on their site to answer questions when nobody's around. It runs on the same Cloudflare Worker and Llama 3 setup as the sidebar. Clients get a Backstage dashboard to update the AI's knowledge without touching code.

The difference from a typical agency is that there's no agency. You work with one person directly, which is how custom work ends up at a fraction of what an agency would charge. Every project is built start to finish by the same person who quoted it.

There are a few live client deployments at this point — a fine art and studio pottery site, a 3D printing manufacturing company (The Chop Lab), an artisanal goods shop, and a fine arts visual archive. Each one is a serverless edge SPA on Cloudflare, built on the same infrastructure as the Worker that runs the sidebar AI.

Minescout Beta

Beta is its own thing entirely. beta.minescout.net launched in early 2025 as a platform for testing and reviewing AI tools — a place to actually use emerging models, document what they're good at, and be honest about where they fall short. It's where a lot of the model literacy that later informed architecture decisions came from. Some of that output made it onto Life as posts: the AI comparison series, the deep research comparisons, the image generation battles.

Technically it's unlike anything else in the stack. The whole interface is a terminal — green text on black, matrix rain canvas in the background, CRT scanlines, the works. Navigation is a command panel that opens with /. Articles render as fake nano editors. There are hidden files that only appear with ls -a, an access level system, physics commands, easter eggs. It's deliberately more of an experience than a site. Firebase runs there for auth — the last place in the MineScout stack that still uses it, and not for much longer.

The Coding Projects

The standalone apps that lived as HTML files in the old site — GeoMaster, the Vigenère cipher, the AI number games — are accessible through the coding projects section of Life. They weren't migrated into the JSON post system. They're more like tools than articles. GeoMaster Pro is a geography quiz. The Vigenère cipher is a working implementation of the polyalphabetic cipher. The AI number games were built to test how well specific models handle constrained reasoning tasks. The posts about them are in the timeline. The apps are still running.

What the Stack Looks Like Now

Across the whole MineScout presence there are four live sites, a Cloudflare Worker handling the AI layer, a second Worker handling the client backend for Minescout AI, and a PM2 process keeping the Life dev server alive permanently on the origin. The portfolio at minescout.net runs vanilla JS, no build step. Life runs Vite 8 + React 19, no database. The client sites run as serverless edge SPAs on Cloudflare. Beta runs its own terminal stack with Firebase for auth. None of these share infrastructure in any meaningful way — each one was built for what it needed at the time.

That's the same philosophy that produced a 27,000-byte index.html on the old Life site, so it's worth being honest about: the bias toward "build the simplest thing that works" cuts both ways. The React rebuild happened because the simplest thing had stopped working. The Cloudflare architecture exists because serverless edge genuinely is the right answer for low-traffic sites that still need global performance. Firebase stayed on Beta because nothing broke badly enough to justify replacing it.

What's Next for Life

Three things are still on the list. Search is the one that matters most — with 32 posts across five categories and three years, there's no good way to find something specific without scrolling. A client-side search over the manifest JSON would be fast and require nothing new on the backend. The archive pages currently just filter the homepage by year; real archive pages would give each year its own URL and proper context. The feature request board is the most open-ended and will probably start simple — a form that appends to a JSON file, same pattern as everything else.

Nothing about the deployment changes. No build step. No pipeline. Write the post, hit save, it's live.

This post was written with the help of Claude Sonnet 4.6 — who read six zip files, a 154,000-byte views.js, a Firebase-powered terminal interface, and a lot of diff output before writing a single word. The code, the decisions, and the work are mine. Claude handled the synthesis.
